transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. It's nice to meet you too. Um, I guess I came in because I've been having a really hard time lately with... well, with how I look. There's this spot, just around my nose and cheek, where it looks uneven to me. I see it every time I take a photo, and the fluorescent lights at the store where I work as a cashier just make it look so obvious. I keep getting stuck on it. My friends and family tell me they don't see anything wrong, but I just can't shake the feeling that it's the very first thing every customer and my manager notices when they look at me. It's just really starting to bother me.
How certain are you that other people notice this uneven spot as much as you do?

Um, I guess I'm not entirely certain. I mean, my family and friends say they don't see it, and no customer has ever actually pointed it out or anything. But... when I'm standing there under those bright lights, I just feel like everyone is staring right at it. It's hard to believe they don't see it when it looks so obvious to me. So, I don't know for sure, but it definitely feels like they do.
How often do you check or try to hide the uneven spot in mirrors, photos, or other reflections?

Well, pretty often, I guess. Especially at work. Like, on my breaks, I almost always end up going to the bathroom just to check my face in the mirror. I'll stand there and try fixing my hair around it to sort of cover the spot up. And... I also catch myself comparing my face to the girls who come through my checkout line. Sometimes I get so caught up checking the mirror and adjusting my hair that I actually take way too long, and I end up being late getting back to the register.
Do you have any repetitive rituals or checking behaviors that are unrelated to your appearance?

Um, no, not really. I don't think so. I mean, I don't have any other habits like that. It's really just the stuff with my face and the mirror. I don't feel the need to check locks or wash my hands a certain number of times or anything like that, if that's what you mean. It's just... just my appearance that I get stuck on.
When you are in social situations, do you worry about being judged or embarrassed even when you are not thinking about your appearance?

No, not really. If I'm not thinking about my face, I'm usually fine around other people. I don't really worry about saying the wrong thing or, like, embarrassing myself in general. It's really just... the uneven spot. That's the only thing that makes me feel like people are judging me. If I could just fix that, I wouldn't worry about being around people at all.
How long have you been preoccupied with the uneven spot on your face?
I'm not really sure exactly when it started, to be honest. I guess it's been a while, but I don't have a specific timeline or anything. It's just something I've been focused on for some time now.
On a typical day, about how much time do you spend thinking about or checking the uneven spot?"

Um, it kind of adds up throughout the day. Like, when I'm at work—I work as a cashier—on my breaks I always end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror. I'll spend time fixing my hair around it, trying to hide it. And even when I'm working, I catch myself comparing myself to the girls who come through my checkout line. Sometimes I take so long looking in the mirror on my break that I'm actually late getting back to the register. So, I guess it's a pretty good chunk of time.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient is preoccupied with a perceived facial defect that others do not observe and engages in repetitive mirror checking, camouflage, and appearance comparisons. The preoccupation causes distress and occupational impairment, supporting body dysmorphic disorder. Social anxiety disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder were considered but are less consistent because the concerns are specifically appearance-focused and no broader social fears or non-appearance obsessions/compulsions were reported.

Frequent mirror checking during work breaks
Repeatedly adjusting hair to conceal the perceived defect
Comparing facial appearance with other women
Spending so much time checking and adjusting appearance that she is late returning to the register
Significant distress about the perceived facial irregularity
Occupational interference resulting in lateness returning to the cashier register
